name: Printing A Sequence of Repeated Numbers (Case 2)
description: Construct a program that receives an integer N from the user and prints a sequence of space-separated numbers from 1 to N such that the N-th number in the sequence is repeated N times.
code:
#Step 1: Read the integer N that the user enters
N = int(input("Enter the integer N: "))
#Step 2: Print N space-separated numbers
for i in range(1, N+1):  
    #Step 2.1: Print the i-th number i times
    for j in range(1, i+1): 
        print(i)

1.content: #Step 1: Read the integer N that the user enters

commentList: You read what the user types and store it as an integer in the variable N so the later loop knows how far to run.
The input('Enter the integer N: ') part shows a prompt and returns a string; int(...) converts that string to an integer; the = assigns the result to N.

A common mistake is to assume input() returns a number — it returns text, so forgetting int(...) will break the loop. Also, if the user types non-integer text or a decimal like '3.5', int(...) will raise a ValueError and the program will crash.

To be safe, you should validate the input. For example, wrap the conversion in a try/except and ask again on error, or check the text before converting. Note that simple checks like str.isdigit() don't handle negatives.
Stylistic tips: use a lowercase name like n by convention, and avoid including prompts when your program will be auto-graded (use input() with no prompt in that case).
This line starts the outer loop that steps through each number i from 1 up to and including N; you use i as the current number that will be printed i times.

Syntax breakdown: range(1, N+1) creates a sequence starting at 1 and stopping before N+1, so the values produced are 1, 2, ..., N; the trailing colon (:) begins the indented block that is the loop body.
Semantics: for each value of i produced by range, the loop runs once and then the inner loop (on the next lines) prints i exactly i times — the outer loop controls which number is being repeated.

Common errors and misconceptions: if you used range(N) you would start at 0 and miss printing N; if you used range(1, N) you would miss the last number N; forgetting the colon or wrong indentation causes a SyntaxError or logical mistakes.

Edge cases to watch: if N is zero or negative the loop body will not run at all, so you should validate N if you expect positive input; also very large N can make the program slow or produce huge output.

Best practices: consider a clearer variable name like num instead of i to show intent, ensure the inner loop is correctly indented under this line, and validate the input (e.g., require N > 0) before entering the loop.

5.content: #Step 2.1: Print the i-th number i times

commentList: Purpose: This inner for-loop makes the program run the indented block exactly i times so that you print the current number i, i times.
Syntax/semantics: 'for j in range(1, i+1):' means you create a loop variable j and iterate over the numbers 1 through i inclusive; the colon starts the loop body that will run once per j.
Why i+1 is needed: range(a, b) stops before b, so you use i+1 to include i. A common mistake is using range(1, i) which runs only i-1 times.
About the loop variable j: you don't actually use j inside the body here — it's only a counter. If you want to show that j is unused, you can name it '_' to make your intent clearer.

Common errors: forgetting the trailing ':' causes a SyntaxError; wrong indentation will break the nesting (so the inner loop must be indented under the outer loop); using range(i) starts j at 0 which may be confusing if you expect 1..i.

Best practices: if you want the final output to be space-separated (as the problem asks), you should print with print(i, end=' ') or build a list and join it, because print(i) alone adds a newline each time. Also, for large N consider building strings instead of many small prints for performance.
Edge cases: if i is 0 or negative the loop does nothing (no repetition), and if you expect only positive N you should validate the input before the loops.
Purpose: this line prints the current number i each time the inner loop runs, so you get i printed i times (once for each iteration of j).
Syntax and meaning: print(i) calls Python's print function with the value of i. The parentheses are required in Python 3, and print will output the value of i followed by a newline by default.
Common misconception: you might think you should print j (the inner-loop counter). If you printed j, you would show the inner index (1..i) instead of the outer loop value i that you want repeated.

Potential error to watch for: because print() adds a newline, this code will put each number on its own line rather than space-separated. If you want space-separated output, use print(i, end=' ') and after the loops print() once to move to a new line.
Indentation matters: this line must be indented inside the inner for-loop. If you unindent it, you'll print i only once per outer loop instead of i times.

Best practice for large N: printing inside nested loops can be slow. If you need better performance or precise spacing, collect the values in a list (e.g., append str(i) each time) and print them once with ' '.join(list). This also gives you full control over separators.

You might choose this because it looks like it iterates up to i and skips an extra step you think is unnecessary. However, range(1, i) produces values 1 through i-1, so the inner loop runs only i-1 times instead of i. That means each number i will be printed one time too few (for example, when i = 4 you'll get three prints instead of four). The program will run without a syntax error, but the output will systematically under-repeat every number by one, so the N-th number will appear N-1 times rather than the required count.

commentList: You might pick this because it seems natural to reuse N as the number of repetitions. But using range(1, N+1) makes the inner loop iterate N times for every value of i. As a result, every number from 1 to N will be printed N times, producing far more repeats than intended (total prints = N * N). For example, if N = 3 you would print nine numbers instead of the intended pattern. The program will still run, but the pattern of repetitions will be incorrect because the inner loop no longer depends on the current i.

commentList: You might choose this distractor because it looks like a simple relationship between N and i and seems to control the number of inner iterations. However, using range(1, N-i+1) makes the inner loop run N-i times (and zero times when i equals N), so the program will produce a decreasing number of repeats (many repeats for small i and none for the last i) instead of printing the i-th number i times. This causes the final number to be omitted and the whole repetition pattern to be inverted. The distractor thus misunderstands the needed loop bound: it ties repetitions to the remaining count rather than to i, producing wrong counts and an empty inner loop for i = N, so it is invalid for the intended behavior.

commentList: You might pick this because it looks like a range expression and uses N, so it feels related to repeating a number. The mistake is that it reuses the outer loop variable i for the inner loop and computes bounds using N instead of making the inner loop run exactly i times. That reuse overwrites the outer i and breaks the outer loop’s progression, and the end bound N-i+1 can be ≤ start so the inner loop often does nothing. In short, this distractor reflects a confusion about loop variables and loop bounds: it won’t reliably repeat the current number i the correct number of times and will produce wrong or missing output.

commentList: You might choose this because many examples start ranges at 0, so it feels safe. However, range(0, i+1) yields i+1 iterations (0 through i), so the inner loop runs one extra time. That causes each number i to be printed i+1 times instead of i. For example, when i = 3 you'll print the number 3 four times. The program won't crash, but every repetition count will be too large by one, so the output pattern will be wrong.
